title: The Influential British Psychologist You've Probably Never Heard Of
author: Marc Smith
summary: Smith uses the forgotten career of William Henry Winch to argue that the gap between educational research and classroom practice is not a modern complaint but a structural one, identified and attacked more than a century ago. Winch was a London pupil teacher who qualified as a schoolmaster, taught science in an East End elementary school, then took unpaid leave to read psychology at Cambridge, and in 1900 published Problems in Education protesting what he called the divorce of psychological theory from applied education. His proposed remedy was institutional: train education students who held both disciplines at once and could judge which parts of each usefully combined. Between 1905 and 1913 he worked without pay on full time educational research, contributing more papers to the British Journal of Psychology than anyone else in the period, and he ran controlled experiments in real classrooms with real teachers, using parallel and correlated group designs, matched groups, correlation, and replication. Smith explains the obscurity as a double penalty: Winch built no theory and straddled two fields, so neither educational practice nor academic psychology claimed him, and his findings on phonics based reading and on early school entry conferring no academic advantage went unadopted. He sets the dismissive verdict of Sharp and Bray against Collins's assessment that Winch ran probably the most sustained empirical memory programme in pre 1914 Britain. The closing irony is that the post Winch's work helped create went to Cyril Burt in 1913, and Winch became an instance of the very problem he had named.
points: Winch's 1900 complaint about the divorce between psychological theory and applied education is presented as the same research to practice gap teachers still face.
His proposed fix was a new kind of trained person, the education student competent in both psychology and schooling, rather than better dissemination.
He ran his experiments inside ordinary schools with teachers and pupils rather than in laboratories, using matched and parallel group designs and attempting replication.
Smith attributes his erasure to his refusal to theorize and his position between two disciplines, neither of which adopted him.
Winch's findings that early school entry gave no academic advantage and that a phonics based reading system worked were both largely ignored despite favourable results.
quotes: There’s always been a mismatch between educational research and educational practice. Several studies have found that while students continue to use ineffective learning methods, educators are still likely to recommend them.

During his time working for the Inspectorate, he published Problems in Education (1900), espousing his dissatisfaction with what he saw as the divorce between psychological theory and applied education.

One of his particularly interesting proposals was the introduction of education students, individuals trained in both education and psychology, capable of judging which features of the two disciplines could be usefully combined.

Experience of schools speedily convinced me that what was needed in England was a group or groups of workers competent in psychology, experimental or otherwise, of their day, and also with much knowledge of schools and school conditions, having, as it were, a foot in either camp
First, he wasn’t building a theory. Winch wanted to discover what would help teachers teach more effectively, rather than construct theories attempting to explain how memory worked.

He used controlled experiments in actual classrooms rather than conducting them in a laboratory and only then attempting to implement findings in the real world. He utilised teachers and students, compared groups, progressed to using correlation, developed matched-group designs, and attempted replications.
Winch was not a great psychologist. It is indeed arguable that had he remained a schoolteacher all his life, the history of educational psychology would not have been vastly different
Ultimately, he became a symptom of the problems he first highlighted in Problems in Education, problems that, to a large extent, persist today.
